raw_response:
I am 66 years old and I have farmed these 11.9 mu in Quzhou for 45 years. I never went to school, but I know this land with my hands and my eyes. There are three of us in my household — me, my husband, and our son, who works part-time in town but comes back for harvest and planting. We have a well, so we can irrigate, but pumping costs electricity and money, so I only water when the crop really needs it. I always grow wheat in winter and maize in summer on the same land. That is what my neighbors do and what my parents did. It is the only way I know to get two crops a year and have enough to eat and a little to sell.

For wheat this season, I will buy improved seeds from the seed shop in town. The old local seeds do not yield enough anymore. I will plough the field after the maize stubble is cleared, because wheat likes a deep, soft bed. At planting I will spread compound fertilizer — about one big bag for every two mu — and then topdress with urea when the wheat turns yellow at jointing. If I do not feed it then, the ears will be small. I will irrigate three times: once after sowing so the wheat can settle before winter, once at jointing when it shoots up, and once when the grain is filling. I also spray herbicide once after sowing, and insecticide once if I see aphids. Last year I got about 1000 jin per mu; this year I hope for the same, around 500 kg per mu, if the frost does not damage it.

For maize, the time after wheat harvest is very short — sometimes only five or six days. I will use hybrid seeds, because without hybrid maize you get nothing worth harvesting these days. I will hire the rotary tiller to come the same day the wheat is threshed, and plant the next day. I put compound fertilizer in the planting furrow, and then add urea when the maize is about knee-high. Maize needs water at tasseling and grain-filling, so I will irrigate twice. Pumping twice is enough if the rains are normal. I spray herbicide once and insecticide once. I expect about 1200 jin per mu, which is about 600 kg.

I do not change my methods much. Last year was not bad, so I will do the same this year. I do not have money to try new things and fail. My neighbor uses about the same amounts, and if it works for her it works for me. I would rather put a little too much fertilizer than too little — a thin crop means we go hungry. But I also cannot buy more than I can afford, so I stick to what I know.
